title: Trading on an Exchange
lessons/crypto-u3-l1/steps/0/body: In **spot**, you buy the actual coin and **own it**, so you can withdraw it to your own wallet. You only profit when the price **goes up**, and since there's no leverage, you can't get **liquidated** either.
lessons/crypto-u3-l1/steps/1/body: In **futures**, you don't buy the coin itself; you open a **contract** on its price. You can go **long** (profit when price rises) or **short** (profit when price falls), and use **leverage**. The most common type in crypto is the **perpetual**: a contract with no expiry date.
lessons/crypto-u3-l1/steps/1/tip: On perpetuals, a "funding" payment passes between longs and shorts every few hours, so holding a position for a long time can cost you.
lessons/crypto-u3-l1/steps/2/prompt: Which of these can you do in futures, but not in regular spot?
lessons/crypto-u3-l1/steps/2/options/0: Go short to profit from a price drop
lessons/crypto-u3-l1/steps/2/options/2: Withdraw coins to a personal wallet
lessons/crypto-u3-l1/steps/2/options/3: Hold coins for the long term
lessons/crypto-u3-l1/steps/2/explanation: In regular spot, you only profit when the price rises. Shorting is what contracts are for. On the flip side, withdrawing coins to a wallet only works in spot, because only there do you own the coin.
lessons/crypto-u3-l1/steps/3/pairs/2/mea: Futures contract with no expiry date
lessons/crypto-u3-l1/steps/3/pairs/3/mea: Forced close of a leveraged position
lessons/crypto-u3-l1/steps/4/body: With **10x leverage**, every 1% price move means a 10% gain or loss on your margin. If price moves about **10% against** you, your whole margin is gone and the position gets **liquidated**. In practice it happens a little sooner, because the exchange also counts **maintenance margin** and fees.
lessons/crypto-u3-l1/steps/5/prompt: You went long with 100 USDT margin at 10x, and price rose 3%. Roughly what's your profit (before fees)?
lessons/crypto-u3-l1/steps/5/explanation: Your position is 100 × 10 = 1,000 USDT, and 3% of 1,000 is 30 USDT: a 30% gain on your margin. The same multiplier works on losses too.
lessons/crypto-u3-l1/steps/6/statement: In spot trading without leverage, your position gets liquidated if price falls 50%.
lessons/crypto-u3-l1/steps/6/explanation: There's no liquidation in spot. You're down 50% on paper, but the coin is still yours. Liquidation only happens when you trade with leverage.
lessons/crypto-u3-l1/steps/7/prompt: You went long at 60,000 with 10x leverage, and price is falling. Roughly what level is the "?" line?
lessons/crypto-u3-l1/steps/7/explanation: At 10x, a drop of about 10% (from 60,000 to around 54,000) wipes out your whole margin. Because of maintenance margin, liquidation hits a little above 54,000. Your stop loss should sit well before this line.
lessons/crypto-u3-l1/steps/8/prompt: A beginner wants to hold Bitcoin for a few years. Which approach makes more sense?
lessons/crypto-u3-l1/steps/8/options/0: Buy spot and move it to a secure wallet
lessons/crypto-u3-l1/steps/8/options/1: Open a 50x long on futures and forget it
lessons/crypto-u3-l1/steps/8/options/2: Go short because the fees are lower
lessons/crypto-u3-l1/steps/8/options/3: A futures position with no stop loss
lessons/crypto-u3-l1/steps/8/explanation: For long-term holding, spot makes sense: you own the coin, you can't get liquidated, and you don't pay recurring funding. High leverage can wipe out everything with the first sharp move.
lessons/crypto-u3-l2/steps/0/body: The **order book** is the list of limit orders waiting to be filled. The **buy side (bid)** shows the prices buyers are offering, and the **sell side (ask)** shows the prices sellers want. The gap between the best bid and the best ask is called the **spread**.
lessons/crypto-u3-l2/steps/1/prompt: In the Ethereum order book, the best bid is $3,000 and the best ask is $3,001.5. What's the spread?
lessons/crypto-u3-l2/steps/1/explanation: 3,001.5 − 3,000 = $1.5. The more liquid a market is, the tighter its spread usually is.
lessons/crypto-u3-l2/steps/2/body: A **limit order** that doesn't fill right away **adds liquidity (maker)** to the order book. A **market order** fills instantly at the best available prices and **takes liquidity (taker)**. Many exchanges charge makers lower fees.
lessons/crypto-u3-l2/steps/3/statement: A market buy order gets filled by orders on the sell side (ask) of the order book.
lessons/crypto-u3-l2/steps/3/explanation: When you market buy, you start with the cheapest sellers. If your order is big, you climb step by step to higher prices.
lessons/crypto-u3-l2/steps/4/body: **Liquidity** is how many orders sit near the current price. If the order book is **thin**, a big market order eats through several levels and your average price gets worse. This is called **slippage**.
lessons/crypto-u3-l2/steps/5/prompt: The sell side of the order book has these two levels. You buy 2 ETH with a market order. What's your average buy price?
lessons/crypto-u3-l2/steps/5/explanation: (3,000 + 3,010) ÷ 2 = $3,005. The first level only had 1 ETH, so the second half of your order filled at a higher price.
lessons/crypto-u3-l2/steps/6/prompt: This is an illiquid altcoin. Tap the candle where a big market sell order probably wiped out several levels of buyers in the order book at once.
lessons/crypto-u3-l2/steps/6/explanation: In a thin market, a big market sell fills buyers across several levels in a row, and price suddenly drops 8%. Then new orders pull price back up, leaving a very long lower wick on high volume.
lessons/crypto-u3-l2/steps/7/prompt: You want to buy a large amount of an illiquid altcoin. What reduces slippage?
lessons/crypto-u3-l2/steps/7/options/0: Buy with limit orders in several smaller chunks
lessons/crypto-u3-l2/steps/7/options/1: One huge market order, all at once
lessons/crypto-u3-l2/steps/7/options/2: Buy only the moment big news drops
lessons/crypto-u3-l2/steps/7/explanation: A limit order locks in your price, and buying in pieces keeps you from eating through several order book levels at once.
lessons/crypto-u3-l2/steps/8/sentence: A ___ order adds liquidity to the order book, and a ___ order takes it away.
lessons/crypto-u3-l2/steps/8/explanation: A limit order waits in the order book (maker); a market order fills instantly against existing orders (taker).
lessons/crypto-u3-l3/steps/0/body: Three common costs: the **trading fee** (a percentage of every buy and sell, like 0.1%), the **withdrawal fee** (for moving coins off the exchange) and the **network fee**, which goes to miners or validators. Withdrawal fees usually depend on the network.
lessons/crypto-u3-l3/steps/1/prompt: You buy 500 USDT of Bitcoin and later sell it for 500 USDT. Each trade has a 0.1% fee. How much did you pay in fees in total?
lessons/crypto-u3-l3/steps/1/explanation: Each trade costs 0.5 USDT in fees, so the round trip is 1 USDT. The more you trade, the more fees you pay.
lessons/crypto-u3-l3/steps/2/body: A coin like USDT lives on several networks (**ERC-20** on Ethereum, **TRC-20** on Tron, and more). **Your withdrawal network must match the receiving network.** Otherwise your funds could get lost, or getting them back could be hard and expensive.
lessons/crypto-u3-l3/steps/2/tip: Ethereum addresses start with 0x and Tron addresses start with T: a quick check that you picked the right network.
lessons/crypto-u3-l3/steps/3/statement: If you send Tether over TRC-20 and the destination only supports ERC-20, it's no problem, because both are Tether.
lessons/crypto-u3-l3/steps/3/explanation: These are tokens on two separate blockchains. Sending on the wrong network can end with your funds lost.
lessons/crypto-u3-l3/steps/4/prompt: You want to send Tether from an exchange to a wallet whose deposit address starts with T. Which network do you choose?
lessons/crypto-u3-l3/steps/4/explanation: Addresses that start with T belong to the Tron network, so you should choose TRC-20.
lessons/crypto-u3-l3/steps/5/body: Copy the address and check its **start, end and middle** against the original; some malware swaps copied addresses. Some coins also need a **memo (or tag)** when you deposit to an exchange. For big amounts, send a small **test transaction** first.
lessons/crypto-u3-l3/steps/5/tip: Blockchain transactions can't be reversed. There's no "cancel" button.
lessons/crypto-u3-l3/steps/6/prompt: Put the steps of a safe transfer from an exchange to your personal wallet in order.
lessons/crypto-u3-l3/steps/6/items/0: Copy the address and network from the receiving wallet
lessons/crypto-u3-l3/steps/6/items/1: Paste the address on the exchange and pick the same network
lessons/crypto-u3-l3/steps/6/items/2: Check the pasted address against the original
lessons/crypto-u3-l3/steps/6/items/4: Once it arrives, send the full amount
lessons/crypto-u3-l3/steps/6/explanation: First pin down the destination, then enter and check the address. A small test transaction proves everything works before you risk the full amount.
lessons/crypto-u3-l3/steps/7/pairs/0/mea: Deposit ID that some coins require
lessons/crypto-u3-l3/steps/7/pairs/1/mea: A small amount sent before the real one
lessons/crypto-u3-l3/steps/7/pairs/2/mea: Cost that goes to miners or validators
lessons/crypto-u3-l3/steps/7/pairs/3/mea: A percentage of every buy and sell on an exchange
lessons/crypto-u3-l3/steps/8/prompt: You want to send 2,000 USDT to your wallet. Your wallet only supports ERC-20, but the exchange charges more to withdraw on ERC-20 than on TRC-20. What's the best move?
lessons/crypto-u3-l3/steps/8/options/0: Send via ERC-20; a higher fee beats losing your funds
lessons/crypto-u3-l3/steps/8/options/1: Send via TRC-20; it's cheaper and Tether is Tether
lessons/crypto-u3-l3/steps/8/options/2: Send on any network; the exchange will fix mistakes
lessons/crypto-u3-l3/steps/8/options/3: Skip checking the address so it arrives sooner
lessons/crypto-u3-l3/steps/8/explanation: The network must match what the destination supports. A few extra dollars in fees is nothing next to the risk of losing 2,000 USDT. Check the address too, and send a test amount first.
